source.title: Linear RNN Scaling Laws: When Longer Sequences Beat More Sequences
source.authors: Zi-Yan Chen; Zhong-Zhu Zhou; Lin-He Zheng; Pei-Lin Liu; Ding-Xuan Zhou

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study derives scaling laws and runs synthetic experiments aimed at the same scaling questions, but uses a sketched linear-RNN teacher–student model and squared prediction risk rather than empirical scaling sweeps of language models.
record.gate_note: The paper tests theoretical risk scaling in a synthetic autoregressive model. It does not test actual language-model held-out cross-entropy or report predictions of much larger runs from fits to smaller runs. Cited empirical long-context and language-model results are background, not results of this study.
record.test_reason: The paper builds a stylized theory of scaling laws. It proves and numerically checks power laws for squared prediction risk in a synthetic system: a Gaussian latent linear-RNN teacher with a sketched linear recurrent student, trained by full-batch GD. No language model (or any neural network) is trained, and no held-out pretraining cross-entropy, extrapolation, real compute-optimal split, architecture shape or downstream task is measured. Every version is stated for language models or neural models in other modalities. The results therefore bear on a related but different system and are recorded under fits_no_version, not as tests. The paper cites the empirical LM laws (Kaplan, Hoffmann) only as motivation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that their sketched linear-RNN model yields risk scaling laws in M, N·P and R, separated by spectral crossovers. When θ≥α the known one-scale rates are recovered and N and P are interchangeable. When α−2r≤θ<α, longer trajectories also suppress the initialization transient, so longer sequences beat more sequences. They also derive compute-optimal allocations with token-limited and token-rich phases.
record.recipe_differences: A theoretical teacher–student model with Gaussian sketches, linear recurrent prediction, squared population risk, and full-batch safeguarded WSD gradient descent; it is not an empirical transformer pretraining sweep using held-out cross-entropy.
record.method_sensitivity: The scaling changes with the relative initialization and innovation spectral exponents (θ versus α) and, in Regime II, with trajectory length P across representation, optimization, and variance crossovers.

fits_no_version.finding: In a sketched linear-RNN teacher–student model, the approximation, GD-bias and variance components of squared prediction risk follow power laws in M, R, N and P. Measured slopes are near the theory guides, e.g. −0.962 vs −0.90 and −1.008 vs −1.0, but bias vs R gives −0.718 vs −0.60.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Solvable linear sequence models reproduce power-law risk scaling in model dimension, data and optimization time.

fits_no_version.finding: When the initialization spectrum has the heavier tail (θ<α), the scaling exponents change across P-dependent crossovers. Trajectory count and length then stop being interchangeable: variance falls as P^−1.253 versus N^−0.986.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sequence length and number of sequences are not interchangeable data budgets when early-context transients carry heavy-tailed structure.

fits_no_version.finding: Under fixed compute C = DM²L, the toy model's optimal width, tokens and steps grow as powers of C. The exponents depend on the spectral exponents α and θ, and a token-limited vs token-rich phase split appears.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute-optimal allocation exponents in solvable models depend on data-spectrum exponents.

record.problems: Evidence is from a stylized Gaussian linear-RNN model rather than real language models. Experimental sweeps cover limited synthetic parameter ranges; fitted-slope uncertainty is not stated. The held-out quantity is squared prediction risk, not cross-entropy.

untested.parts: No language-model held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; only squared risk in a linear toy model.
No fit on small runs used to predict larger runs.
No empirical compute-optimal parameter/token split for neural LMs; the allocation is derived only for the synthetic model.
No other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer with neural models.
No comparison of parameter counting, schedules, data or fitting methods for LM laws, and no published exponents compared.

missing.what: Regime I token-limited allocation: D*≍T, M*≍γC/T², L*≍T³/(γ²C), critical budget T_crit,I≍(γC)^((α+1)/(2α+3)).
Regime II checkpoint ratios of measured to guide values (approx mean 1.000; bias mean 0.987; variance means 1.037, 0.983, 1.030).

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with V1, V3 and V7 links over-reads a purely theoretical toy model as evidence about language-model scaling. No neural network is trained. Experiments only verify the paper's own theorems in synthetic Gaussian linear systems, and fitted-slope uncertainties are not given. The Regime-I bias slope deviates notably from its asymptotic guide (−0.718 vs −0.60).

versions.untested_parts: The measured quantity is population squared prediction risk and its approximation, optimization-bias, and variance components in a synthetic linear-RNN model—not held-out cross-entropy of real language models. No sweep of joint training compute is reported as a loss-versus-compute curve.
No power law fitted on small runs is used to predict the loss of much larger runs.

The compute-optimal allocation is derived for the paper’s synthetic model and asymptotic conditions, not validated on language-model training runs. In Regime I the leading-order split between trajectory count N and sequence length P is not determined.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer experiments.

The study demonstrates dependence on the primitive covariance spectra and sequence length in its model, but does not compare parameter-count conventions, fitting methods, real-data choices, or published empirical exponents.

rows.subject: synthetic stable linear-RNN teacher–sketched linear recurrent student (Regime I)
rows.operation_detail: Varied sketch dimension M and fitted the approximation-risk slope.
rows.measure: Log–log slope of approximation risk versus M
rows.note: The quantity is a component of the synthetic model’s population squared prediction risk, not cross-entropy.
rows.check: Approximation risk of a synthetic sketched linear model, not LM loss. The baseline is the paper's own asymptotic guide (−0.90); the measured −0.962 deviates about 7% from it. Move to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: synthetic stable linear-RNN teacher–sketched linear recurrent student (Regime I)
rows.operation_detail: Varied optimization steps L, reported against effective horizon R.
rows.measure: Log–log slope of GD-bias risk versus R
rows.note: This is optimization bias in the synthetic risk decomposition.
rows.check: GD-bias component in the synthetic model, not LM loss. The measured slope −0.718 differs from the reference −0.60 by about 20%, which the record's 'observed' glosses over.

rows.subject: synthetic stable linear-RNN teacher–sketched linear recurrent student (Regime I)
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of independent trajectories N.
rows.measure: Log–log slope of empirical variance versus N
rows.uncertainty: Variance error bars are standard errors across sketch-level means; slope uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: The reported variance is the empirical variance component of the synthetic population risk.
rows.check: Variance component vs trajectory count in the synthetic linear model; not a language-model loss measurement.

rows.subject: synthetic stable linear-RNN teacher–sketched linear recurrent student (Regime I)
rows.measure: Log–log slope of empirical variance versus P
rows.uncertainty: Variance error bars are standard errors across sketch-level means; slope uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: The paper says N and P have the same leading inverse-token effect in Regime I.
rows.check: Synthetic variance vs P in Regime I. The V7 link is also wrong even on the reader's own logic: this Regime-I row shows N and P interchangeable, not setup-dependence of LM laws.

rows.subject: synthetic stable linear-RNN teacher–sketched linear recurrent student (Regime I)
rows.measure: Log–log slope of empirical variance versus R
rows.uncertainty: Variance error bars are standard errors across sketch-level means; slope uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: The paper attributes the increase to optimization activating additional noisy directions.
rows.check: Variance increasing with optimization horizon in the synthetic model; not LM loss.

rows.subject: synthetic stable linear-RNN teacher–sketched linear recurrent student (Regime II)
rows.operation_detail: Varied trajectory length P and fitted the approximation-risk slope.
rows.measure: Log–log slope of approximation risk versus P
rows.baseline: Two-scale guide slope −0.950 on the same grid
rows.uncertainty: Approximation error bars are standard deviations across sketches; slope uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: The two-scale guide is M^(1−βα) + P^−1 M^(1−βθ).
rows.check: Synthetic Regime-II approximation vs P. It measures the paper's two-scale guide, not fitted LM exponents or published-law disagreement.

rows.subject: synthetic stable linear-RNN teacher–sketched linear recurrent student (Regime II)
rows.operation_detail: Varied trajectory length P and fitted the GD-bias slope.
rows.measure: Log–log slope of empirical bias versus P
rows.uncertainty: Bias error bars are standard deviations across sketches; slope uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: The paper reports that longer trajectories reduce bias in this initialization-dominated regime.
rows.check: Synthetic GD-bias vs P; not an LM measurement.

rows.subject: synthetic stable linear-RNN teacher–sketched linear recurrent student (Regime II)
rows.measure: Log–log slope of empirical variance versus N
rows.uncertainty: Variance error bars are standard errors across sketch-level means; slope uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: This N sweep is compared with the Regime-II P sweep in r9.
rows.check: Synthetic variance vs N; it matches −1 as in Regime I. The V7 link is not supported by this row alone.

rows.subject: synthetic stable linear-RNN teacher–sketched linear recurrent student (Regime II)
rows.measure: Log–log slope of empirical variance versus P
rows.uncertainty: Variance error bars are standard errors across sketch-level means; slope uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: The paper says the stronger-than-P^−1 decay reflects both the larger token budget and suppression of the initialization transient; thus N and P are not interchangeable in Regime II.
rows.check: Synthetic variance vs P (−1.253 vs guide −1.250); a toy-model result, not LM fitting choices.

rows.subject: synthetic stable linear-RNN teacher–sketched linear recurrent student (Regime II)
rows.measure: Log–log slope of empirical variance versus R
rows.uncertainty: Variance error bars are standard errors across sketch-level means; slope uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: The reported variance is the empirical variance component of the synthetic population risk.
rows.check: Synthetic variance vs R; not LM loss.

rows.subject: synthetic stable linear-RNN teacher–sketched linear recurrent student (Regime II)
rows.operation_detail: Derived the approximation-risk crossover as sequence length changes.
rows.value: Approx ≍ M^(1−βα) + P^−1 M^(1−βθ); equivalently, M^(1−βα) + P^−1 M^(1−βθ) switches dominance at mP = P^(1/(α−θ)).
rows.note: This is an analytic result for the model, with a sequence-length-dependent crossover rather than one regime-independent expression.
rows.check: Analytic theorem statement, not a measured result. The crossover is in M at mP = P^(1/(α−θ)); the record's value restates it confusingly. Not LM fit-dependence.

rows.subject: synthetic stable linear-RNN teacher–sketched linear recurrent student (Regime II)
rows.operation_detail: Derived the optimization-bias crossover as sequence length changes.
rows.value: Bias ≍ R^((1−βα)/α) for R ≲ RP; Bias ≍ P^−1(R/P)^((1−βθ)/θ) for R ≳ RP.
rows.note: The theorem gives different bias dependences on the two sides of the sequence-length-dependent crossover.
rows.check: Analytic theorem (bias crossover at R_P = P^(α/(α−θ))) for the toy model; not an empirical measure on LMs.

rows.subject: synthetic stable linear-RNN teacher–sketched linear recurrent student (Regime II)
rows.operation_detail: Derived the effective-dimension and variance crossover as sequence length changes.
rows.value: Var ≍ (NP)^−1 min{M, R^(1/α)} for R ≲ RP; Var ≍ (NP)^−1 min{M, (R/P)^(1/θ)} for R ≳ RP.
rows.note: The formulas retain the NP factor but change the effective dimension across the crossover.
rows.check: Analytic variance theorem for the toy model; not an LM measure.

rows.subject: synthetic stable linear-RNN teacher–sketched linear recurrent student (Regime I)
rows.operation_detail: Analytically optimized model dimension, used transitions, and optimization horizon under fixed compute.
rows.value: D⋆ ≍ (γC)^((α+1)/(2α+3)); M⋆ ≍ (γC)^(1/(2α+3)); L⋆ ≍ γ^−1(γC)^(α/(2α+3)); no leading-order preference for P⋆, with N⋆ = D⋆/P⋆.
rows.note: The aggregate transition budget and model dimension follow compute power laws, but the leading-order N/P split is not selected.
rows.check: Analytic compute-optimal allocation for the synthetic model (C = DM²L), not an LM parameter/token split. Only the token-rich branch is recorded; the token-limited Regime-I branch is omitted.

rows.subject: synthetic stable linear-RNN teacher–sketched linear recurrent student (Regime II)
rows.operation_detail: Analytically optimized model dimension, sequence length, trajectory count, and optimization horizon under fixed compute and a token cap.
rows.note: The allocation is stated up to asymptotic constants and within the theorem-controlled regime.
rows.check: Analytic token-limited allocation in the toy model; not validated on any trained network.

rows.subject: synthetic stable linear-RNN teacher–sketched linear recurrent student (Regime II)
rows.operation_detail: Analytically optimized model dimension, sequence length, trajectory count, and optimization horizon under fixed compute.
rows.note: The paper also states that the token-rich optimum lies at P⋆ ≍ (M⋆)^(α−θ) and R⋆ ≍ (M⋆)^α.
rows.check: Analytic token-rich allocation in the toy model. Exponents depend on the synthetic spectra α and θ, not on LM setup or fitting choices.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Synthetic Regime I and Regime II risk-component sweeps
reader_labels.reason: The reported approximation, bias, and variance slopes closely follow the stated power-law guides in the tested synthetic settings (r1–r10); these are not real-language-model cross-entropy results.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The derived allocation gives power-law growth in compute for model dimension, trajectory count, and sequence length in this regime (r16).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Model dimension and total transitions have compute-power allocations, but the paper finds no leading-order preference for the split between N and P (r14).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Different primitive spectra and trajectory-length regimes in the synthetic model
reader_labels.reason: Regime II has P-dependent approximation, bias, and variance crossovers, and its variance response to P differs from Regime I (r4, r6–r9, r11–r13).
